script.opening_words: Your bank knows exactly how much money you have and based on that number, just that number, it's already decided what kind of person you get to be. The fees you pay, the rates you get, whether your call gets answered or sent to a 40-minute hold, whether your deposit clears today or in five business days, whether the suit guy walks out of the back office to greet you or whether you stand in line behind a velvet rope

script.analysis: Full 15705 canonical characters read. A single-character narrative explainer: hook (balance decides who you are), the inverted borrowing gap (36% vs 6%), Mike at $800 (fees, CFPB 9%/79%, repeal, subprime card, call centres), $20,000-$100,000 tiers, Citigold and wealth advisers, Chase Private Client, million-dollar mortgage discounts and luxury perks, cross-subsidy argument, private banking above $3M, securities-backed lending and buy-borrow-die with ProPublica figures, and a close on fee awareness. Most structural and regulatory claims check out; fee arithmetic, the Indigo fee, SBLOC range and Bezos per-$100 figure are wrong or inconsistent.

claim_audit.assessment: CFPBOD: the 9%/79% split is verified from CFPB data as cited by CRS. The under-$350 balance figure appears in Senate floor remarks (Congressional Record, 26 March 2025), not confirmed against the CFPB study.

claim_audit.assessment: CFPBOD: verified. The final rule (December 2024) capped fees at $5 for banks over $10 billion unless cost-justified; S.J.Res. 18 passed the Senate 27 March and House 9 April 2025 and was signed 9 May 2025 under the Congressional Review Act. "Proposed" understates that it was a final rule.

claim_audit.claim: ProPublica: the 25 richest Americans gained $401 billion in 2014-2018 and paid $13.6 billion, a 3.4% true tax rate; Bezos 0.98%; a typical American paid $160 per $100 of wealth growth.

claim_audit.assessment: PROPUB: $401B, $13.6B and 3.4% verified; Bezos 0.98% verified. K02: 13.6 / 401 = 3.39%. The script then says Bezos paid "about $1.09" per $100, which contradicts its own 0.98%. The $160 comparison is consistent with ProPublica's median-household example (analyst recall).
